text: Lesson 1 turned Priya's request into a written scope. This lesson splits that scope into the two concrete migrations it's actually made of, and just as importantly, says what's deliberately left out.

The catalog app migration is really two separate problems wearing one sentence. The static assets -- Driftwood's product images, sitting as files on the on-prem server's disk -- need a new home that can serve them over the web reliably. And the VM workload -- the application code that renders catalog pages -- needs a new server to run on, configured close enough to the original to behave the same way. One's a storage problem, one's a compute problem, and each already has a known pattern.

In scope: a resource group, a storage account for the images, a virtual machine for the app server, basic monitoring, end-to-end testing, documentation, and a cutover plan presented to Priya before the actual switch.

Out of scope, on purpose: re-architecting the app into containers or something serverless -- this is a lift-and-shift, not a rewrite. High availability or auto-scaling -- one well-monitored VM is the right size for this ask. Any other application Driftwood runs. And automated CI/CD pipelines -- real, valuable work, just not what this deadline needs.

Before opening the Azure Portal or CLI, sketch the target in one plain-English paragraph: one resource group, one storage account with a container for images set to a fast-loading tier, one virtual machine running the catalog app reachable the way the on-prem server was, and basic monitoring watching its health. If you can't describe it that simply, you're not ready to start provisioning yet.
With the scope and target sketch written down, next lesson turns that paragraph into real Azure resources -- the resource group, storage account, and VM, provisioned for real.
